newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: Cambodian parliament set to vote on new premier.
newsitem.headline: Cambodian parliament set to vote on new premier.

text.p: The Cambodian parliament on Wednesday will vote for a new first prime minister to replace ousted Prince Norodom Ranariddh despite constitutional difficulties that throw the validity of the process into question.

Foreign Minister Ung Huot has been nominated by members of Ranariddh's FUNCINPEC party remaining in the country to replace the prince as co-premier. Second Prime Minister Hun Sen, who ousted the prince on July 6, backs Ung Huot's nomination.
Assembly officials said on Tuesday that a vote by secret ballot on Ung Huot's nomination would be held on Wednesday.
The vote would be preceded by a show of hands on suspending the prince's parliamentary immunity in order to clear the way for his prosecution for alleged crimes, a senior assembly official said.
After taking sole power, Hun Sen said he wanted to keep his Cambodia People's Party's coalition with FUNCINPEC in place and that FUNCINPEC should select a new first prime minister.
Hun Sen has also said he was committed to holding free and fair elections scheduled for May.

But political analysts said despite Hun Sen's efforts to be seen to be doing things by the book, there were articles in the constitution making it difficult to push through Ung Huot's selection as first prime minister fully in accordance with the charter. But few people were expected to object.
"To select Ung Huot you have to violate the constitution, no doubt about it," said one political analyst.
"Inside the country no one will object, outside, yes, they will," he said referring to Ranariddh and his supporters.
Hun Sen ousted Ranariddh on July 6 after two days of fighting in the capital. The prince had left Cambodia two days earlier and has been calling for opposition to Hun Sen from abroad.
Hun Sen said the prince, if he returns to Cambodia, must face charges stemming from his negotiations with the Khmer Rouge guerrilla group and for alleged weapons smuggling.

Many FUNCINPEC members and sympathisers left the country after the prince's ouster, including some 20 members of the 120-seat parliament, either representatives of FUNCINPEC or a smaller allied party.
According to the Cambodian constitution, the king should approve a new first premier after receiving agreement on a nomination from the assembly's president and its two vice presidents.

King Norodom Sihanouk said late last month he would not recognise Ung Huot as first premier as the post belonged to Ranariddh. The king also said that a vote on a new first prime minister by an incomplete parliament would be invalid.

"The decisions of an incomplete parliament working under conditions of very questionable 'freedom' and 'regularity' could not be considered valid within the spirit of our 1993 Constitution and our liberal democracy," the king said in a comments faxed to news agencies in Beijing, where he is receiving medical treatment.
Complicating the picture is that one of the assembly's vice presidents fled to Bangkok after the prince's ouster and has said he does not agree with Ung Huot's nomination.
But Chan Ven, deputy secretary general of the National Assembly and a member of Hun Sen's party, brushed aside the possible complications.
"The National Assembly is the supreme body," he told reporters.
A delegation from the Association of South East Asian Nations (ASEAN) asked for clarification on points in the constitution and in FUNCINPEC party rules during talks with Hun Sen at the weekend.
ASEAN postponed Cambodia's membership in the group after Hun Sen's takeover and said it still recognised the prince as first prime minister.
The United States said it did not recognise Ung Huot's nomination by an incomplete FUNCINPEC party.
